info.desc: Aladdin Sane is the sixth studio album by the English musician David Bowie, released on 13 April 1973 through RCA Records. The follow-up to his breakthrough The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars, it was the first album he wrote and released from a position of stardom. It was co-produced by Bowie and Ken Scott and features contributions from Bowie's backing band the Spiders from Mars — Mick Ronson, Trevor Bolder and Mick Woodmansey — with pianist Mike Garson, two saxophonists and three backing vocalists. Recorded in London and New York City between legs of .

podcast.body: Bowie's mid-1970s character was named "Aladdin Sane," a title that reflected his mental state during that period, punning on "A lad insane." "No wonder Bowie's mid-70s characters was named Aladdin Sane."

podcast.body: One of Bowie's peak glam era LPs that topped the British album chart but did not hit number one in America. It was one of his last UK number one LPs until "Scary Monsters." "And though he hadn't had a UK number one LP, since the era of Aladdin, Sain, and Diamond Dogs, even Bowie's quirkier LPs from the Berlin period, consistently made the UK top five."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.body: Released in 1973, this album further twisted Bowie's alien persona and made his look even more iconic, notably with its album cover featuring a bear-chested, flame-haired David with lightning bolt face makeup and a teardrop. Although its lead single "The Jean Genie" wasn't a big US pop hit, the potency of Bowie's persona ensured the album sold well, leaping into the top 20 and hitting number 17 by June 1973. "And they were joined by a new album that put a twist on Bowie's alien persona and made his look even more iconic, Aladdin's scene."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.body: Released on April 13, 1973, this album was Bowie's first as a "genuine rock star." The "Aladdin Sane" character served as a transitional persona, evolving the "Ziggy Stardust" concept to a "higher realm" and being further developed through subsequent albums, even if not explicitly named Ziggy. "The Gene Genie written in part about his even crazier friend, Eiki Pop, and inspired by Jean Genie. Another friend who was a writer, poet, and political activist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released on April 13th, 1973, this was Bowie's first album as a "genuine rock star" and further developed the Ziggy persona into a "higher realm." The title itself, when separated as "A Lad Insane," hinted at Bowie's mental state and was influenced by his half-brother Terry's struggles with mental illness. "The next album, also called Aladdin Sane, was Bowie's first as a genuine rock star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
